identity.title: Food Safety Plan for Ready-to-Eat Hummus and Bean Dips

page_refs.issuer: not issued by an agency; prepared by Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager

scan.summary: This is Willamette Valley Foods' Food Safety Plan under the FDA's Preventive Controls for Human Food rule (FSMA). It describes the company's written hazard analysis and preventive controls for ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips made at the Salem plant, covering cooking, cooling, sanitation, allergen management, and metal detection. The plan is the company's own document—not issued by the FDA or Oregon Department of Agriculture—and it establishes what the company must do and record to stay in compliance.
scan.freshness_note: Document effective date is May 12, 2025. As of today (September 25, 2026), the plan is about 16 months old and should be reviewed for continued accuracy. Food safety plans must remain current and be updated if the process, ingredients, or identified hazards change. No revision date is given; ask whether it has been reviewed or revised since May 2025.

gaps.title: No allergen hazard for other sesame-containing ingredients
gaps.description: The plan identifies sesame allergen hazard only for tahini at receiving. However, lemon juice, garlic, olive oil, and spices can also contain sesame from co-packing or cross-contact. If any of these ingredients are not from dedicated facilities or certified allergen-free, sesame cross-contact is a realistic hazard not analyzed.
gaps.fix: Expand the hazard analysis to identify sesame or other allergen hazards for all ingredients that carry risk. Add to the supply-chain program a requirement for allergen statements or allergen-free certifications from all ingredient suppliers, not just tahini and dry beans.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.126(b) requires hazard analysis to include allergens; 21 CFR 117.80 requires supplier verification for hazards.
gaps.quote: Products are made from cooked chickpeas or black beans, tahini, lemon juice, garlic, olive oil, salt and spices

gaps.title: No preventive control for sesame cross-contact from non-sesame products
gaps.description: The plan requires allergen labeling review and product scheduling with hummus items last, followed by full washdown. However, there is no preventive control for cross-contact during the blending or filling of non-sesame bean dips if they are made on the same line earlier in the day. If both sesame and non-sesame products use the same blender or filling equipment, sesame residue could contaminate the non-sesame product before the washdown.
gaps.fix: Clarify whether sesame and non-sesame products can use the same equipment. If yes, add a control: either (a) run all non-sesame products after washdown and sesame products first, or (b) validate that the washdown removes all detectable sesame allergen between products. Document the validation or the equipment separation procedure.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.126(b) and FDA Guidance on Allergen Cross-Contact; 21 CFR 117.80(b) requires written procedures to prevent cross-contact.
gaps.quote: product scheduling with hummus items last in the day, followed by full washdown

gaps.title: Cooling time limit may not be science-based for this product
gaps.description: The plan requires cooling from 135°F to 70°F in 2 hours and 70°F to 41°F in a further 4 hours. This is a standard time-temperature guideline from guidance documents, but it is not justified for legume-based dips with the specific formulation, water activity, or pH stated in the plan. A HACCP or FSMA plan should cite the scientific basis or validation that supports the chosen limits for this specific product.
gaps.fix: Add a sentence or citation stating the source of the cooling time limits (e.g., reference FDA/USDA Clostridium perfringens guidance, or cite a validation study specific to this product). If no such validation exists, commission or reference a peer-reviewed study that validates these limits for the product's formulation and container size.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.126(a)(2) requires the hazard analysis to be based on scientific evidence; 21 CFR 117.126(c) requires preventive controls to have a scientifically sound basis.
gaps.locator: Section 4 (Preventive controls) — Spore-former growth at cooling row; Section 3 (Hazard analysis) — Cooling row
gaps.quote: Cool cooked beans from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours and to 41°F within a further 4 hours in the blast chiller

gaps.title: No critical limit for cooking temperature accuracy
gaps.description: The plan specifies a minimum internal temperature of 212°F for 60 minutes, measured with a calibrated probe thermometer, but does not state the required accuracy or margin of error for the thermometer. FDA guidance expects ±2°F accuracy. If the thermometer drifts, the actual product temperature might fall short of the lethal dose for Salmonella or Listeria.
gaps.fix: Add to the critical limit: 'Probe thermometer calibration tolerance: ±2°F.' This should appear in Section 4 under the cook control, or add a separate requirement in Section 7 specifying that calibration must verify accuracy to ±2°F.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.80(b) and FDA Compliance Program Guidance on food safety inspections, which expects ±2°F accuracy for process-critical thermometers.
gaps.locator: Section 4 (Preventive controls) — Vegetative pathogens at cook row; Section 7 (Verification)
gaps.quote: measured with a calibrated probe thermometer

gaps.title: No frequency or criteria for review of trend data
gaps.description: Section 7 states that environmental monitoring results are trended quarterly, but does not define what action is taken if a trend shows increasing Listeria spp. detection, or how many consecutive quarters of elevated results trigger an investigation or process change.
gaps.fix: Add acceptance criteria for environmental monitoring trends, such as: 'If any site shows positive Listeria spp. results in two consecutive quarters, or if two or more sites are positive in a single quarter, a root-cause investigation is initiated and documented.'
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.126(c) requires preventive controls to include procedures for monitoring effectiveness; 21 CFR 117.170(b) requires sanitation controls to be verified.
gaps.quote: Environmental monitoring results are trended quarterly.

gaps.title: Missing re-test interval for finished product Listeria testing
gaps.description: Section 7 states finished product is tested for Listeria monocytogenes monthly, but does not define the lot size, sample size (how many packages per lot), or acceptance criteria (zero tolerance, or a stated limit). This leaves ambiguity on whether a single positive result triggers product recall or whether multiple positives are tolerated.
gaps.fix: Add specifics: 'Monthly finished product testing: minimum [X] samples per production lot of [Y] tubs. Acceptance criterion: zero Listeria monocytogenes detected. If any sample is positive, the entire production lot is recalled or destroyed, and the corrective action is investigated.'
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.80(b) and 21 CFR 117.170 require written procedures for verification of preventive controls, including acceptance criteria.
gaps.quote: Finished product is tested for Listeria monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory.

gaps.title: No procedure for responding to a positive Listeria in finished product
gaps.description: Section 6 (Corrective actions) does not address what happens if the monthly finished product test is positive for Listeria monocytogenes. Only environmental monitoring positives are addressed. A positive finished product result is a critical failure and requires immediate action, traceability, and likely market notification.
gaps.fix: Add to Section 6: 'If finished product is positive for Listeria monocytogenes: (1) the entire lot is held; (2) production is halted; (3) an investigation of the environmental monitoring, sanitation, and process records from that production date is completed within [X] hours; (4) a recall determination is made in consultation with the quality manager and plant manager; (5) FDA and relevant retail customers are notified within [X] hours; (6) root cause is documented and corrective actions taken before production resumes.'
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.126(c) requires preventive controls to include corrective action procedures; 21 CFR 117.160 requires written recall procedures.
gaps.locator: Section 6 (Corrective actions) — not in the document

gaps.title: No written recall procedure
gaps.description: The plan does not include a written recall procedure or contact list for customers, the FDA, or Oregon Department of Agriculture. 21 CFR 117.160 requires this.
gaps.fix: Add Section 11 (or expand corrective actions): Recall Procedure. Include: names and phone numbers of key contacts (plant manager, quality manager, FDA regional office, Oregon DEA); definition of recall scope (production lot, date range, SKU); notification template and timeline; records to retain; post-recall verification.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.160(b) requires a written recall procedure and a written list of recall contacts.

gaps.title: No product traceability or lot tracking detail
gaps.description: The plan describes date coding but does not specify lot code format, how lots are traced back to ingredient lots or production runs, or how a product recall would identify all affected packages.
gaps.fix: Add to Section 1 or 9: 'Lot coding: [format, e.g., MMDDYY]. Traceability: Each production run is assigned a unique identifier linking the lot code to ingredient lot numbers, production date, time, and shift. Records of ingredient lot numbers are retained with production records for [at least 2 years].'
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.160(c) requires the ability to trace back and trace forward each article of food produced.
gaps.locator: Section 1 (Facility and product description) or Section 9 (Records)
gaps.quote: filled, sealed, coded and held refrigerated

gaps.title: No training documentation procedure
gaps.description: Section 10 states all production employees receive food hygiene training at hire and annually, but does not require documentation or describe the content. If an inspector asks, there must be evidence (sign-in sheets, certificates, training records) showing who was trained, when, and on what topics.
gaps.fix: Add to Section 10: 'Training records: All training is documented with the employee name, date, topic, and trainer signature or initial. Records are kept for at least [2 years] in personnel files at the plant. PCQI training certificates are copied into the employee file.'
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.190 requires written procedures for training and maintenance of training records.
gaps.quote: All production employees receive food hygiene training at hire and annually.

gaps.title: No preventive control for incoming ingredient verification beyond supplier audit
gaps.description: Section 8 requires suppliers to provide third-party audit certificates and certificates of analysis, but does not require the company to verify that the audit is current (how many years old is acceptable?), conduct receiving inspections, or test incoming lots for allergens, pathogens, or foreign material before use.
gaps.fix: Expand Section 8: 'Supplier verification: Suppliers must hold a current third-party audit (no older than [2 years]). Receiving inspections: Each incoming lot of tahini and dry beans is inspected for signs of contamination, damage, or pest activity. High-risk lots [define criteria, e.g., new suppliers, or lots exceeding [X] months storage] are tested for [pathogens/allergens/metal] by an accredited lab before release to production.'
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.80(c) requires written procedures for supplier verification of hazards; 21 CFR 117.126 requires preventive controls for identified hazards.
gaps.quote: Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot.

gaps.title: No defined water quality or use specification
gaps.description: The plan does not address water used in cooking, cooling, blending, or sanitation. If the plant uses well water or recirculated cooling water, microbiological quality must be verified. FDA guidance expects water quality testing if water is a process input.
gaps.fix: Add to Section 8 or 1: 'Water: [a] If municipal water is used, annual verification of potability is obtained from the water supplier. [b] If well water or recirculated cooling water is used, microbiological testing (coliforms, Listeria) is performed quarterly. Results are maintained as records.'
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.37 and 21 CFR 117.80(b) require controls for water used in food manufacturing.
gaps.locator: not in the document; should be added to Section 1 or 8

scan.confidence_notes: HIGH CONFIDENCE: Document is clearly readable, complete, and well-structured. The plan covers the required elements of 21 CFR Part 117 Subpart C (Preventive Controls for Human Food): hazard analysis, preventive controls with critical limits, monitoring, corrective actions, verification, and records. The facility information, product description, process flow, and hazard analysis are specific and grounded in the company's operations. MEDIUM CONFIDENCE in several areas: (1) Cooling time-temperature limits (135→70°F in 2 hours, 70→41°F in 4 hours) are standard but not explicitly validated for this product's formulation or container size; (2) No scientific basis or reference is cited for these limits; (3) Thermometer calibration tolerance is not specified (±2°F is industry standard but not stated in the plan); (4) Finished product Listeria testing protocol lacks sample size, lot size, and acceptance criteria; (5) Environmental monitoring trend criteria are not defined (no action triggers for increases). LOWER CONFIDENCE regarding: (1) Whether the sesame allergen hazard analysis is comprehensive for all ingredients, or whether other minor allergens (nuts, soy, mustard in spices) are present and unaddressed; (2) Adequacy of supplier verification—plan does not require pathogen testing of incoming dry beans or sesame; (3) Cross-contact control between sesame and non-sesame products—product scheduling and washdown ATP are named but validation is not mentioned. NO GAPS relating to: (1) The legality of the plan itself—it appears to satisfy the structural and procedural requirements of 21 CFR 117.126 through 117.190; (2) Compliance with Oregon state food safety law (not reviewed separately, but no state-specific gaps are evident); (3) The competence or qualifications of the PCQI (March 2024 FSPCA training is current). AREAS NOTED AS 'NOT IN DOCUMENT' but which may be on file elsewhere: Approved supplier list, sample cook/cooling/monitoring logs, lab test reports, calibration records, training documentation, corrective action logs, or other records. The plan is the control document; the records are separate. RECENCY: Effective date is May 12, 2025; as of September 25, 2026, the plan is approximately 16 months old and should be reviewed for any process, ingredient, or product changes.
